10:23 Discussion of LLMs and their development

• The video discusses how Grok, founded in 2015, has become a leader in LLM (Large Language Models).

14:08 Discussion on the use of LLM in various fields

• The video discusses various companies that use LLM to create chatbots and other applications.
• Issues related to the use of LLM are discussed, such as cost of operation and scalability.

• The video discusses Grok's plans to deploy 1.5 million LPU (Large Processing Units) by the end of next year.

comments.author: @Urgelt
comments.text:
FLOPs are interesting as a measure of efficiency.

Not as a measure of model strength.

There are ways to improve model strength without more compute. You know this is true, Wes.

Agentization is one.

Data curation is another. Has it escaped your notice that models can be trained to do their own data curation? Throwing out bad data cuts compute requirements and improves model quality.

It's all iterative. Even if compute were fixed, models will get better.

Better compact models are coming. The most interesting part of your report today was the efficiency gains in Grok. Better results for the compute cycles invested.

(I refuse to spell it 'Groq.' Too cutesy, and maybe it dishonors Robert Heinlein a bit, too. Give the man his due. We needed a word for 'deep understanding,' and he gave it to us.)

comments.text:
I think everyone overestimate Llama-3 70b and for their proof just bring up lmsys chat arena. Let me remind you that chat arena's leaderboard is based on the public votes, so, overhyped models that receive more upvotes than another model they're competing with will get to the higher ranks (on 0:23 you can see that Llama-3-70b-Instruct got only 1599 votes in comparison to other models that have more votes). And don't tell me that 'you don't know what model you're voting for' since you can vote in the side-by-side mode where you can specifically select what models should compete against each other.

My point is, don't believe benchmarks, don't believe leaderboards, don't believe hypetrains that are spread around social media.
Try the model yourself for your use cases and see if it's performing good.
Personally, i think that Llama 3 is definitely a good starting point for improvement in finetuning for your datasets.
But, i would still keep using Claude 3 Opus, since this model just has a bigger context length, which is a must-have for programming. And, in terms of performance, they aren't that different, so i don't see any reason to switch.

An important distinction to make when comparing running models on laptops, then moving on to the Groq "chip", is that the when Groq is producing around 500tps, it's actually running on over 500 Groq chips in parallel - each chip only has 230MB sram. So it's unlikely Groq will affect the consumer GPU market at all as models grow. Server farms? maybe, if their pricing radically changes.

There's a some easily digestible comparisons between the H100 and Groq here which outline this far better than I could. - essentially one H100 is around 5 Groq chips and a groq chip costs around half of one H100 from tsmc
